To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) parasite species richness increases with fish longevity, (2) parasite species benefit from fish longevities, (3) there is an energetic trade-off in female fish between reproduction and immune function, (4) there is no immunohandicap in male fish, and (5) parasite species benefit more from females with low gonad size than from females with high gonad size.
(1) fish mortality is a factor contributing to fish parasite species richness and (2) parasite abundance is related to host spleen size and reproduction in females.
the parasite species richness is negatively related to the host mortality and the parasite abundance is positively related to the fish spleen size.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the relationship among parasite species richness, host life history traits, immune defence and reproduction in cyprinids.

the relationships between parasite diversity and host longevity, and between reproduction and immunity in fish, and it contributes to a better understanding of the mechanisms that regulate the host–parasite interactions in natural systems.
the role of life history traits, parasite diversity and immune function in fish reproduction.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the energetic trade-off between reproduction, immunity and parasitism is a complex process, which is dependent on many factors.
the trade-off between immunity and reproduction is not straightforward and that it depends on the sex of the host, the life history traits, the type of immune function and the type of parasite.

parasite species richness and abundance are related to fish life-history traits, and that the trade-off between reproduction (in females) and immunity is related to the energetic costs of reproduction.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the trade-off between reproduction (fecundity) and immunity (spleens size) in fish females is related to the energetic costs of reproduction, whereas the trade-off between immunity and growth is related to the costs of immunity.
parasitism influences fish life history traits, but the effect is not consistent with predictions based on the immunocompetence handicap theory.
parasite species benefit from fish with a long life history, while parasite species richness and parasite abundance were negatively correlated with fish reproductive investment.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the trade-off between reproduction, immune function and parasitism is a complex issue and that the results of the analyses are dependent on the species studied, their ecology and life history traits.
the relationship between parasitism and fish life history traits should be investigated in a comparative way using a large number of host species.
parasitism is not a negligible phenomenon for fish life history evolution.
